title: Soundscape: A Construct of Human Perception

findings.quote: environmental sound can be interpreted as a resource composition that can elicit diverse affective reactions.
A listener is not only a passive receiver of environmental noise; instead, a listener becomes part of a dynamic system of information exchange and is involved in its creation.

findings.antecedent: Physical environment (bottom-up process, e.g., SPL reduction)
findings.quote: Noise control engineering still uses this simplified concept and still strives to reduce annoyance strictly by minimizing the sound pressure level of unwanted noise. Any interactivity of this process is neglected, and any multidimensionality is discarded.
the notion that the perception of an environment involves an interaction between the individual and said environment has long been established

findings.consequent: Explanation for complex perceptions (e.g., auditory/visual illusions)
findings.quote: There are numerous examples of auditory or visual illusions that demonstrate elementary sensations are not sufficient to provide an explanation for these perceptions, such as the influence of the color of a train on judgements of loudness

The person cognitively constructs the environment to a certain extent through knowledge-driven information processing. In contrast to the simplistic bottom-up concept, top-down controlled perception causes human perception and responses are not determined only by external physical stimuli.

findings.consequent: Perceptual organization of scenes and ability to detect important events
findings.quote: Attention-related factors (i.e., sustained attention to an entire auditory scene, selective attention to particular objects or streams within a scene, attention switching, or attention limitations) can have dramatic influences on the perceptual organization of scenes and the ability to detect important events in the environment.

findings.consequent: Perceived objects being placed in a category and given meaning
findings.quote: through recognition, perceived objects are placed in a category and are given meaning
Human perceptions of physical environments lead to a few basic emotional dimensions, which are indicative of human feelings and are thought to be independent of each other.
the affective quality of sounds that elicit physiological reactions does not correlate with the intensity of those sounds.

findings.antecedent: Understanding how a place influences a person emotionally
findings.quote: the understanding of the acoustical properties of a certain place is far less important than understanding how that place influences a person emotionally.

findings.consequent: Relevance for survival and well-being, preparation for action
findings.quote: emotional stimuli and emotional responses represent a special type of stimulus-response as they possess high relevance for survival and well-being, potentially preparing the individual for action

findings.consequent: Unconscious emotions, influence on behavior, well-being, and health
findings.quote: soundscapes frequently elicit unconsciously emotions, which exert influence on individuals' behavior, well-being, and health.

findings.consequent: Variance explained by acoustical properties (e.g., SPL)
findings.quote: only one-third of variance in annoyance data can be explained by acoustical properties of the sound, usually determined in terms of overall, time-averaged, sound pressure levels

findings.antecedent: Salient sounds in the sonic environment
findings.consequent: Capture attention and contribute to soundscape appraisal
findings.quote: Sound events that are salient and stand out in the sonic environment capture our attention and contribute highly to the perception and the appraisal of the soundscape

findings.antecedent: Social and cultural background of the individual
findings.consequent: Perception and assessment of environmental noise
findings.quote: the perception and assessment of environmental noise depends on the social and cultural background of the individual
assessment of a soundscape is affected by expectations in several different ways, including the aspects of behavior and control

findings.antecedent: Potential interference with other possible activities
findings.quote: soundscape perception also depended on potential interference with other possible activities at the respective site.
Individuals were less affiliative and less helpful with increasing noise
Attentiveness dropped with increasing noise

findings.consequent: Length of stay at public places
findings.quote: Noise affected the length of stay at public places
Noise (music and speech) affected human serial recall performance
Environmental and classroom noise had a detrimental effect on learning and performance by children
Listening to bird songs decreases walking speed compared to walking with city noise conditions
Moderate levels of ambient noise positively affected creative cognition in contrast to low or high ambient noise levels

findings.consequent: Antisocial behavior, pro-social effects, feeling of safety
findings.quote: Sound can mitigate antisocial behavior, can lead to pro-social effects and increase the feeling of safety

findings.consequent: Agitated behavior in older adults with dementia
findings.quote: Sound can reduce agitated behavior in older adults with dementia

findings.antecedent: Soundscape influences on humans and behavior
findings.quote: these soundscape influences on humans and their behavior in response to the soundscape often take place without being noticed. In many cases, humans are unaware of this special role of sound and they underestimate its impact on behavior and well-being.

findings.consequent: Triggers auditory sensations, interpretation, responses, and outcomes
findings.quote: An acoustic environment triggers auditory sensations. The interpretation of these sensations creates useful information (called auditory perception) that results in responses and an outcome.

findings.consequent: Perception at all perceptual and cognitive stages
findings.quote: Context simply influences perception at all perceptual and cognitive stages.

findings.antecedent: Moods or intentions (formed before encountering stimulus)
findings.quote: a person's response to an environment cannot be completely understood within a strict stimulus-response framework because responses depend on moods or intentions often formed in whole or in part before encountering a specific stimulus and environment

findings.antecedent: Heuristic principles and high-level cognitive effects
findings.consequent: Human construction of perceptions and extraction of meaning from soundscape
findings.quote: Humans construct their perceptions by interpreting sensations and apparently rely on normative principles and on heuristic principles... High-level cognitive effects using heuristic principles are at least as significant as low-level percepts or physical attributes of the signal

findings.antecedent: Retrospective summarized evaluations of past experiences
findings.consequent: Basis for decisions to repeat or avoid
findings.quote: Retrospective summarized evaluations seem very natural because they form the basis on which decisions are made to repeat or avoid past experiences that have direct hedonic consequences

findings.antecedent: Complex streams of varying momentary sensations
findings.consequent: Summary assessment (e.g., judgment on rating scale)
findings.quote: This reduction of complexity is needed to avoid cognitive overload.
people tend to use selected moments of extended experiences to form overall assessments, which is described by Kahnemann (2000) as judgment by prototype.

findings.antecedent: Moment of questioning (in noise annoyance surveys)
findings.quote: self-reported long-term noise annoyance judgments were significantly affected by the very moment of questioning

findings.antecedent: Season (when noise annoyance survey is performed)
findings.quote: the season where a noise annoyance survey is performed has an impact on the annoyance ratings
the construction of an overall assessment goes beyond pure “cognitive averaging" when evaluating a soundscape as a whole

findings.antecedent: Efficient mental representation (grouping objects, reducing complexity)
findings.consequent: Making sense of environment, responding to challenges
findings.quote: Humans must rapidly make sense of their environment to successfully move in the world and respond to its challenges, which might be achieved by creating an efficient mental representation of sensory stimuli by grouping certain objects as equivalent and reducing the complexity of information in the external world.

findings.consequent: Recovery from psychological stress and physiological recovery from sympathetic activation
findings.quote: recovery from psychological stress and physiological recovery from sympathetic activation is faster during exposure to pleasant than to unpleasant sounds
Natural sounds, for example, have the ability to evoke pleasant feelings

findings.consequent: Explanation of induced pleasant feelings from natural sounds
findings.quote: classical indicators related to sound-pressure-level threshold values cannot accurately explain this induced feeling.
positive perceptions of acoustic environments (soundscapes) can be associated with positive health effects.
